name: Jakun
confidence_why: The only statement on Jakun stress is Blagden's 1906 remark, drawn from other collectors' wordlists and hedged as a 'tendency' toward the final syllable across a broad 'Jakun' group, while the modern first-hand phonology of Mohamad Rozi Kasim (2019, 2022, 2023) says nothing about stress at all, so the placement and type of the system remain unknown.
catalog_citation: Skeat, Walter William & Charles Otto Blagden. 1906. Pagan Races of the Malay Peninsula, vol. 2. London: Macmillan. Part IV 'Language' (by C. O. Blagden), 'Grammatical Notes', paragraph 'Accent' (tone remark running onto p. 774); 'Jakun dialects' chapter pp. 400-407 defines Blagden's 'Jakun' group. Open scan: archive.org item.
catalog_locator: vol. 2, p. 773 (archive.org scan, tone sentence completing on p. 774); group label: p. 400 n. and pp. 405-406 ('the Jakun dialects are found only in Johor')
catalog_quote: Accent.—The data with regard to accent and emphasis are very meagre. De Morgan prints the strongly accented part of a word in clarendon and the rest in ordinary type, except “very short” syllables, which he prints in italics. Most collectors fail to mark the accentuated syllable, but it will often be found indicated by an acute accent (') in the spelling I have adopted. As a rule, the accent in all the aboriginal dialects appears to fall on the final syllable. This is most marked, however, in Sakai, where the final syllable is apparently the real root of the word, but the tendency is also traceable in Jakun, even in words of Malayan affinity. This is contrary to Malay usage, but, as in Achinese and Cham, is probably due to Mon-Khmer influence. ... General Characteristics.—Sakai has relatively more monosyllabic or quasi-monosyllabic words (of the iambic type, with the accent on the final syllable) than either Semang or the Jakun dialects, another instance of the closer approximation of Sakai to the Mon-Khmer type. ... There is no evidence of the use of tones in these dialects to differentiate words of otherwise similar sound
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Blagden reports, from collectors' acute-accent marks in wordlists, that accent in the aboriginal dialects of the Peninsula generally falls on the final syllable, and that this final-syllable tendency is also traceable in the Jakun dialects, even in words of Malay origin, contrary to (penultimate) Malay usage. He hedges: the data are 'very meagre' and the pattern 'appears' to hold.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Jakun; for Semang he notes weaker accent, some penultimate accent, and near-even distribution. He adds that there is no evidence of lexical tone in any of these dialects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from wordlists (collectors' acute accents; De Morgan's bold type). Blagden's 'Jakun' is a group label covering Belandas, Beduanda, Mentra, Kenaboi, Jakun proper (Johor) and Orang Laut dialects, all heavily Malay-overlaid; the remark is not a description of a single variety and predates all modern fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statement found (Blagden 1906:773) is made for Blagden's 'Jakun' group as a whole (Belandas, Beduanda, Mentra, Kenaboi, Jakun proper of Johor, Orang Laut; vol. 2 pp. 400-407), not for the modern ISO/Glottolog Jakun [jak / jaku1244] specifically; it is a compiler's inference from other collectors' accent marks on wordlists. The three modern first-hand descriptions opened (Kasim 2022, 2023; TOC of Kasim 2019) all describe Johor Jakun (Kluang, Mersing, Segamat, Kota Tinggi; 'Dialek Jakun Johor Timur/Barat') and are silent on stress.
